Note::TexAccessor::canonicalize_macros¶

Back to Note TeX Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::TexAccessor::canonicalize_macros() const

Normalize Equivalent Built-In Command Spellings¶

canonicalize_macros() rewrites a small, explicit set of legacy or stylistic TeX control words to one canonical spelling. Use it before comparison, indexing, or another source transform when equivalent notation should no longer differ merely because one cell used \dfrac and another used \frac.

The complete mapping is:

Input control word

Canonical output

\dfrac, \tfrac, \cfrac

\frac

\operatorname

\mathrm

\rm

\mathrm

\bf

\mathbf

\it

\mathit

\cal

\mathcal

\Bbb

\mathbb

\lt, \gt

<, >

\leqslant

\leq

Matching is by complete control-word name, not byte prefix. Thus canonical \mathrm remains \mathrm, \item is not mistaken for legacy \it, and an unrelated command such as \ltd is not shortened to <d. Replacements are performed in one lexical pass and are not fed back through the mapping, which makes the result idempotent.

This method does not inspect macro declarations, expand user-defined macros, rewrite arguments, or decide whether two arbitrary commands render alike. Use macro_subs() for declarations and use sites; use collapse_macros() when declarations should be removed without expanding their uses.

The result is a newly owned Text Note with the same rank, shape, and cell order as the receiver. Undefined propagates. Empty cells and cells without a mapped control word are copied unchanged. Bytes and native Bool, Int64, or Float64 Notes reject. The lexical pass is linear in total source bytes and does not compile a regular expression per cell.

Example 1: Every Canonical Family¶

const auto source = pluss::make_note({
    R"(\dfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{a}{b} + \cfrac{x}{y})",
    R"(\operatorname{rank} \rm old \bf b \it i \cal C \Bbb R)",
    R"(\mathrm{kept} \mathbf{v} \item \ltd \leqslant \lt \gt)"});
const auto canonical = source.tex().canonicalize_macros();
std::cout << canonical << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["\\frac{1}{2} + \\frac{a}{b} + \\frac{x}{y}", "\\mathrm{rank} \\mathrm old \\mathbf b \\mathit i \\mathcal C \\mathbb R", "\\mathrm{kept} \\mathbf{v} \\item \\ltd \\leq < >"]

The third cell demonstrates the command boundary: \mathrm, \item, and \ltd survive exactly, while the complete \leqslant, \lt, and \gt commands change.

Example 2: Canonicalization Is Idempotent¶

std::cout << std::boolalpha << "idempotent="
          << (canonical.tex().canonicalize_macros() == canonical)
                 .all().bool_item()
          << '\n';

Output¶

idempotent=true

Example 3: Native Integer Cells Reject¶

try {
  (void)pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{1, 2})
      .tex().canonicalize_macros();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "canonical Int64: rejected\n";
}

Output¶

canonical Int64: rejected

See Also¶

  • collapse_macros: remove declarations and canonicalize the remaining source.

  • macro_subs: substitute locally declared macro bodies at use sites.

  • cmd_sub: rewrite one caller-selected command.
